docs.title: Learning OS
docs.text:
A beginner → professional → expert journey through the machines that run modern software — computers and operating systems, Linux and the shell, networking, Git, containers, Kubernetes, performance, security, and finally AI/ML and the infrastructure that serves it.

Built to a single promise: not just knowledge, but skill. Every topic pairs a short video, a set of standalone notes you never need to rewatch, a guided lab you can run in your browser, and a harder solo lab to prove you can do it alone.

This course is free and public

In the spirit of CS50, freeCodeCamp, and The Odin Project — no login, no paywall. Reuse the framework; the sources are cited so you can go deeper yourself.

docs.title: How each lesson is built (the 8-section loop)
docs.text:
Every lesson follows the same evidence-based loop — one input → retrieve → apply easy → apply hard → self-test → schedule review — so learning compounds instead of leaking away:

Section What you do Why it's there Why this matters See where the topic sits and what it unlocks Motivation + a mental hook Watch One short explainer + terminal casts — watch once A single clear input Key Notes Read the standalone notes The reference you keep; no rewatching Guided Lab Run the steps in a browser terminal Apply it with support Solo Lab Hit a harder goal with only hints Deliberate practice at your edge Self-Check Flashcards + explain-it-back Retrieval beats re-reading Mastery checklist Tick "I can…" — it gates progress Honest proof before moving on Review Come back on day 1 / 7 / 30 Spaced repetition locks it in

The methods behind those sections have names and evidence — see How to learn.

docs.title: How to use this course
docs.text:
You can read it like a book, or work it like a bootcamp. The curriculum was designed around a 4-hour study day; a sustainable daily rhythm is:

Block Minutes What Review 30 Yesterday's flashcards + one older topic (spaced repetition) Theory 60 Watch once, then read the Key Notes actively Practice 105 Guided Lab → Solo Lab; type every command yourself Consolidate 45 Self-check, write 3 things learned, note tomorrow's first question

Short on time? Do less, but keep the loop whole — a 40-minute session that watches, does one lab, and self-checks beats two hours of passive video. Progress is gated by the mastery checklist, not by the clock.

docs.text:
• New here? → Stage 1 · Module 01 — Computer & OS Fundamentals — the front door. Runs in a browser terminal; nothing to install.
  • Want the method first? → How to learn.

docs.title: The map (13 stages, 39 modules)
docs.text:
Foundations → Linux & shell → tooling → programming & networking → containers → Kubernetes → performance → troubleshooting → security & ops → math & CS foundations → data & software engineering → cloud & AI domains → a woven capstone: a Full-Stack AI Service you build, serve, and deploy.

Two things run in parallel

Alongside the lessons you build a homelab — real infrastructure (containers → a Kubernetes cluster → GitOps → observability → GPU model-serving) using the same tools companies run in production. It becomes a public portfolio that showcases your skills for a high-pay job or a business. Every tier has a $0 starting point (your own laptop, or cloud free tiers).

Learning OS is a personal study system, opened up so anyone can learn from it. The full lesson catalogue is published progressively — Module 01 is the complete, runnable pilot.

docs.title: How to learn
docs.text:
The biggest gains in this course don't come from the content — they come from how you study it. Every lesson is deliberately built around a handful of techniques that decades of cognitive-science research show actually work. Learn the techniques once here, then notice them in each lesson's eight sections.

The core idea

You do not learn by putting information in (re-reading, re-watching). You learn by pulling it out (recalling, explaining, doing) — and by spacing that effort over time. Struggle is not a sign the method is failing; it is the method working.

docs.title: The five techniques (and where each lives in a lesson)
1. Retrieval practice (active recall)
docs.text:
Testing yourself is studying, not a check on studying. Trying to recall an answer — even unsuccessfully — strengthens memory far more than re-reading.

  • In a lesson: the Self-Check flashcards and questions; the "explain it back" prompt.
  • Source: retrievalpractice.org (Pooja Agarwal & colleagues) · Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning, Brown, Roediger & McDaniel (Harvard University Press, 2014).

docs.title: 2. Spaced repetition
docs.text:
Review just as you're about to forget. Re-studying at expanding intervals (day 1 → 7 → 30) beats cramming for durable memory.

  • In a lesson: the Review footer with day-1/7/30 dates; each new module reviews one item from an old one.
  • Source: Make It Stick (above); the classic "spacing effect" literature.

docs.title: 3. Interleaving
docs.text:
Mix related topics instead of blocking one at a time. It feels harder — and produces better transfer and discrimination between concepts.

  • In a lesson: review days pull in earlier modules; the connections section links neighbouring topics.
  • Source: Make It Stick; Rohrer & Taylor on interleaved practice.

docs.title: 4. Deliberate practice
docs.text:
Skill grows from focused work at the edge of your current ability, with immediate feedback and targeted correction of weak points — not from comfortable repetition.

  • In a lesson: the Solo Lab (harder, minimal hand-holding); the leveled exercise ladders.
  • Source: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer, Psychological Review (1993) · Peak, Ericsson & Pool (2016).

docs.title: 5. Elaboration & the Feynman technique
docs.text:
Explain an idea simply, in your own words, as if teaching it. Gaps in your explanation reveal exactly what you don't yet understand.

  • In a lesson: the teach-back prompt in Self-Check; the "explain to a 10-year-old" tasks.
  • Source: the Feynman technique (Richard Feynman's learning method); elaborative-interrogation research.

docs.title: Put it together: one honest study loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Watch once] --> B[Read Key Notes actively]
    B --> C[Guided Lab: do it]
    C --> D[Solo Lab: do it alone]
    D --> E[Self-Check: recall + explain]
    E --> F{Could you<br/>explain it cold?}
    F -- no --> B
    F -- yes --> G[Schedule review: day 1 / 7 / 30]
    G --> H[Next topic]

docs.title: Reading is a skill — grow it on purpose
docs.text:
The fastest learners read primary sources: official docs, man pages, specifications, a key book chapter. It feels slow at first and gets faster with reps. Each lesson's Key Notes are written to stand alone, but they always point you to the real source — follow those links. The habit of reading man free, the kernel docs, or an RFC yourself is the difference between knowledge and expertise.

A well-known on-ramp

If you want a guided introduction to these ideas, the free course "Learning How to Learn" (Barbara Oakley & Terrence Sejnowski, on Coursera) is the most popular in the world on this topic and covers focused/diffuse thinking, chunking, and beating procrastination.

docs.title: The one rule
docs.text: Difficulty is the point. When recall feels effortful, when the solo lab makes you think, when the spaced review catches something you'd half-forgotten — that friction is where learning happens. Don't optimize it away.

docs.title: Module 01 — Computer & OS Fundamentals
docs.text: Stage 1 · Foundations · ~2 weeks at 4 h/day · No prerequisites — this is the front door.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A computer stores instructions and data in memory and executes those instructions, one after another, on a processor. An operating system (OS) is the master program that manages the hardware and shares it safely among every other program.

Everything later in this course — Linux, containers, Kubernetes, GPUs, AI infrastructure — is just programs being managed by an OS on hardware. Understand this module deeply and nothing later is magic. Skip it and everything later is memorization.

What this unlocks

Linux is one of these kernels · the shell speaks to the kernel through system calls · Docker is kernel isolation mechanisms · Kubernetes is the scheduler idea at cluster scale · performance tuning is the memory hierarchy with a profiler · AI infrastructure is the accelerator at production depth. Every later module is this one, specialized.

docs.title: Key Notes
docs.text: Standalone. This is the reference you keep.

docs.title: The picture: hardware, kernel, you
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Applications — browser, python, docker"]:::user
    L["Libraries and shells — bash, libc"]:::user
    S{{"system calls — the ONLY door downward"}}:::door
    K["KERNEL — processes · memory · files · network"]:::kern
    D["Drivers"]:::kern
    H["HARDWARE — CPU · RAM · disk · GPU · NIC"]:::metal
    A --> L --> S --> K --> D --> H
    classDef user fill:#eaf0f9,stroke:#2b4c7e,color:#1a1f2e;
    classDef door fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#a9722c,color:#1a1f2e;
    classDef kern fill:#e6f3ef,stroke:#1f7a68,color:#1a1f2e;
    classDef metal fill:#f4f6f9,stroke:#6b7280,color:#1a1f2e;

The user/kernel boundary is the security line of the entire stack: user code is restricted and must ask the kernel — through a system call (open, read, write, fork, execve) — for anything privileged.

docs.title: The six ideas that explain everything
docs.text:
1. Stored program & fetch–decode–execute. Instructions are just numbers in memory; the CPU endlessly fetches the next one, decodes it, executes it. That's all "running a program" is.
  2. Memory hierarchy. Each level is bigger and slower than the one above it. Performance work is mostly "stay near the top."
  3. Process. A running program: its code + its private virtual memory + its state. One program can run as many processes.
  4. Scheduling. The kernel switches the CPU between processes thousands of times a second (context switches), creating the illusion everything runs at once.
  5. Virtual memory. Each process sees its own private address space; the kernel + CPU (MMU) map it to real RAM pages. This is both the protection and the "more memory than RAM" trick — and later the foundation of containers.
  6. Syscalls & privilege. The CPU runs in user mode (restricted) or kernel mode (all-powerful). The split, enforced by hardware, is where all security begins.

docs.title: The memory hierarchy (know these magnitudes cold)
docs.text:
Level Size Latency Registers ~KB ~0.3 ns fastest / smallest L1 / L2 / L3 cache ~MB 1–30 ns RAM ~GB ~100 ns SSD ~TB ~100 µs Network / cloud ~∞ ~ms slowest / biggest

Each jump down is roughly 1000× slower. "Slow" always means waiting on something further down the hierarchy.

docs.title: Power button to running program
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    F["Firmware / UEFI<br/>self-test"] --> B["Bootloader / GRUB<br/>loads kernel"]
    B --> K["Kernel<br/>inits hardware, mounts root FS"]
    K --> P["PID 1 / systemd<br/>starts services"]
    P --> Sh["Login → shell"]
    Sh --> R["You run python3:<br/>fork + execve → process"]

When you type python3: the shell asks the kernel (fork + execve) to create a process; the kernel loads the program and schedules it; every print/read is a syscall; on exit the kernel reclaims everything.

docs.title: Core concepts, compressed
docs.text:
• Everything is numbers — data and instructions and text and pixels, all binary.
  • The CPU is fast but dumb; software is layers of simple steps.
  • Memory is a hierarchy; distance from the CPU = slowness.
  • The OS = sharing + protection + abstraction, enforced by hardware privilege modes.
  • A process is the unit of running software; a file is the unit of stored data.
  • GPUs/NPUs trade flexibility for parallel throughput.

Must remember (if you keep only five things):

  1. A program is a file; a process is that program running (own memory, PID, state).
  2. The OS does three jobs: sharing, protection, abstraction — enforced by user vs kernel mode.
  3. Memory hierarchy: registers → cache → RAM → SSD → network, each ~1000× slower.
  4. A syscall is the only door from user code into the kernel.
  5. Boot order: UEFI → bootloader → kernel → PID 1 (systemd) → services → login.

docs.title: Guided Lab: meet your machine
docs.text:
Basic, step-by-step. Every command here is read-only — it inspects, never changes anything.

▶ Open interactive lab (browser terminal){ .lo-btn } View lab source{ .lo-btn .lo-btn--ghost }

No install needed

The button opens a free Ubuntu terminal in your browser (Killercoda) — no signup, nothing to install. You can also run every command on any Linux machine, or in the terminal cast above.

1 · Your machine2 · Your CPU3 · Your memory4 · Your storage5 · Processes, live 

uname -a       # kernel + architecture
hostnamectl    # machine identity
uptime         # how long it's been running, load average
Record: kernel version, hostname, uptime. Which fact came from the kernel, which from a file?

lscpu
cat /proc/cpuinfo | less
Find: model, cores vs threads, L1/L2/L3 cache sizes, max MHz. Draw the memory-hierarchy pyramid for your CPU.

free -h
cat /proc/meminfo | head -20
Explain total vs used vs available vs cached. Open 10 browser tabs, rerun free -h, explain the change. (High "used" from cache is healthy — read the available column.)

lsblk
df -h
Map the chain: physical device → partition → mount point → your files.

top            # press P (sort by CPU), M (sort by memory), q to quit
sleep 300 &    # start a background process; note its PID
ps aux | grep sleep
kill <PID>     # terminate it; verify it's gone
You just created, observed, and terminated a process through the kernel. What is PID 1?

You can stop here and have learned something real

If you can read your machine's vital signs and run a process through its whole lifecycle, the guided lab is done. Now make it harder.

docs.title: Solo Lab: figure it out
docs.text:
Harder. Goals only — minimal hand-holding. Struggle here is the point; reveal a hint only after you've tried.

Same browser terminal as above. Work each goal before opening its hint.

docs.title: Challenge 1 — Count the context switches
docs.text:
Find out how many context switches your system has performed since boot.

Hint

The kernel exposes live counters as files under /proc. Look for a system-wide stats file.

Solution 

grep ctxt /proc/stat
/proc/stat's ctxt line is the total context-switch count since boot — direct evidence of the scheduler doing mechanism #4, thousands of times a second.

docs.title: Challenge 2 — Reconcile the CPU count
docs.text:
nproc prints a number. Reconcile it exactly with lscpu's cores × threads-per-core × sockets.

Hint

nproc counts logical CPUs. lscpu shows sockets, cores per socket, and threads per core — multiply them.

Solution

nproc == Socket(s) × Core(s) per socket × Thread(s) per core from lscpu. If threads-per-core is 2, hyper-threading is why nproc is double the physical core count.

docs.title: Challenge 3 — Read the error, name the layer
docs.text:
Run ls /root. It fails. In your journal, answer: which layer refused you (hardware? kernel? filesystem permissions?) and why is that refusal correct behaviour?

Solution

Filesystem permissions, enforced by the kernel: /root is mode 700, owned by root. Your unprivileged process is denied by the protection model (mechanism #6) — exactly what should happen. This is security as a feature, not a bug.

docs.title: Challenge 4 (stretch) — 200 processes, one core
docs.text:
top shows hundreds of processes but your machine has few cores. Explain precisely how they all appear to "run at once."

Solution

"Running" mostly means runnable; one core executes exactly one instruction stream at a time, in ~millisecond slices. The scheduler context-switches so fast it looks simultaneous, and most of those processes are actually sleeping on I/O or timers, not competing for the CPU at all.

docs.title: Self-Check
docs.text:
Close the notes. Answer aloud or in writing first, then reveal. Recalling — even when it's hard — is what builds the memory.

Program vs process?

A program is a passive file of instructions on disk. A process is a running instance with its own virtual memory, PID, and state. One program → many processes.

The three jobs of an OS?

Sharing (many programs, few resources), protection (one crash can't kill another), and abstraction ("open file", not "spin disk to sector 5012").

Order by latency: RAM, L1 cache, SSD, network round-trip — with rough magnitudes.

L1 ≈ 1 ns → RAM ≈ 100 ns → SSD ≈ 100 µs → intercontinental network ≈ 150 ms. Each jump ≈ 1000×.

free -h shows 95% used but the machine is snappy. Problem?

Usually not. Most "used" is reclaimable page cache. Check the available column; worry only if available is low and swap is churning.

What is a syscall, and why does it matter for security?

A user program's request for a kernel service — the only door into kernel mode. Because it's hardware-enforced, untrusted code physically cannot touch other processes' memory or devices except through kernel-checked syscalls.

Boot order, power button to login?

UEFI/firmware → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel (mounts root FS) → PID 1 (systemd) → services → login.

Teach it back (the real test)

Out loud, in 2 minutes, no notes: "Explain what an operating system is and why computers need one." You must land sharing, protection, abstraction (any wording). Then, in 90 seconds, teach "memory vs storage" to a 10-year-old — analogy required, jargon forbidden. If you can't yet, that's your signal to reread the Key Notes, not to move on.

docs.title: Mastery checklist
docs.text:
Tick these honestly, cold (no notes). They gate progress to Module 02 — a module is only "done" when every box is true.

  • Explain the three OS jobs with one example each.
  • Draw all four diagrams from memory: the stack, the memory hierarchy, fetch–decode–execute, and boot.
  • Inspect unaided: kernel, CPU, memory, and disks via uname, lscpu, free, lsblk, and /proc.
  • Administer a full process lifecycle: start a background process, find it, inspect it, terminate it, verify.
  • Monitor with top: distinguish CPU pressure vs memory pressure vs idle.
  • Troubleshoot an unseen "slow machine" scenario with stated hypotheses and the right tool order.
  • Debug a given error (Permission denied, or a state-D process) to the correct layer, with reasoning.
  • Secure: explain user/kernel privilege as a security boundary, why sudo demands suspicion, and what /etc/shadow protects.
  • Scale: explain up vs out, and why multicore happened (the ~2005 power wall).
  • Teach: pass the teach-back above (OS explanation mandatory).
  • Read one thing unaided this module — a man page, the kernel docs, or OSTEP ch. 2 — and say what question it answered.

docs.title: Review — lock it in
docs.text:
Spaced repetition is not optional; it's where the memory actually forms. When you finish this module, schedule these and keep them:

When Do Day 1 All flashcards · redraw the stack diagram · one 1-minute "what is an OS" explanation Day 7 All four diagrams from memory · rewrite the inspection commands cold · the security questions Day 30 Reread your own notes and correct anything you now understand better · the two stretch challenges

From Module 02 onward, every review day also pulls in one Module 01 item (a diagram, a question, or a lab redone cold) — that interleaving is what makes it stick.

Connects forward to: Linux (the concrete OS) · the shell (the interface to all of this) · Docker (process isolation) · Kubernetes (the scheduler at scale) · performance tuning (the hierarchy with a profiler) · AI infrastructure (the accelerator, industrialized).

The one-sentence takeaway

Learn Module 01 deeply and the rest of the course is variations on themes you already own.
